exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Component of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthogonal Basis

question.text: Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $100x_2$, where $x_2$ is the second component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$ \[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 25 \\ -3 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}\right\}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2,\,\mathbf{q}_3.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}.$ Computing $x_2,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} x_2 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{q}_2}{\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{q}_2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1 \cdot 25 + 0 \cdot (-3) + 3 \cdot (-4)}{25^2+(-3)^2+(-4)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{25-12}{625+9+16} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{13}{650}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac1{50}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[100x_2=100 \cdot \dfrac{1}{50} =2.\]

question.text: Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $30x_1,$ where $x_1$ is the first component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$ \[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -8 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\right\}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}.$ Computing $x_1,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{q}_1}{\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{-3 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2}{1^2+2^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-3+4}{5} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{5}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[30x_1=30 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5}=6.\]

question.text: Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $5x_1,$ where $x_1$ is the first component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$ \[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\right\}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}.$ Computing $x_1,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{q}_1}{\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5 \cdot (-4) + (-4) \cdot 2}{{(-4)}^2+2^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-20-8}{20} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{7}{5}. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[5x_1=5 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{7}{5}\right)=-7.\]

example.title: Finding a Component of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthogonal Basis

question.text: Given the orthogonal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $\dfrac{x_1}{2}$, where $x_1$ is the first component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$ \[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -14 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right\}, \qquad \mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 57 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2,\,\mathbf{q}_3.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthogonal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}.$ Computing $x_1,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \dfrac{\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{q}_1}{\mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{q}_1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0+57\cdot 7}{1^2+0^2+7^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1+399}{1+49} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{400}{50} \\[5pt] &= 8. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{x_1}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Given the orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ of $\mathbb R^2,$ find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ if $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i.$ Computing the components of $\mathbf{x},$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}= -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{13}}-\dfrac{21}{\sqrt{13}} = -\dfrac{25}{\sqrt{13}}\\[5pt] x_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}= -\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{13}}+\dfrac{14}{\sqrt{13}}= \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{13}} \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{25}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{13}} \end{bmatrix}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Given the orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ - 1 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ of $\mathbb R^2,$ find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ if $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i.$ Computing the components of $\mathbf{x},$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}=0+ 5 = 5 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}= -2+0=-2 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} 5\\ -2 \end{bmatrix}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Given the orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}$ below, find the value of $5x_2$, where $x_2$ is the second component of $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$ \[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 0 \\ \dfrac{4}{5} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{5} \\0 \\ \dfrac{3}{5} \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1\\0 \end{bmatrix} \right\}, \qquad \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ -1\\5 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2,\, \mathbf{q}_3.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i.$ Computing $x_2,$ we obtain

\begin{align*} x_2 &= \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_2 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\-1\\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{5} \\0 \\ \dfrac{3}{5} \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 4+0+3 \\[5pt] &= 7. \end{align*}

Therefore, \[5x_2=5 \cdot 7=35.\]

example.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Given the orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ of $\mathbb R^2,$ find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ if $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i.$ Computing the components of $\mathbf{x},$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}= -\dfrac{6}{\sqrt{10}}-\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{5}} = -\dfrac{11}{\sqrt{5}} \\[5pt] x_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}= -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{5}}+\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{10}}=\dfrac{7}{\sqrt{5}} \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{11}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}.\]

example.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis

question.text: Given the orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ of $\mathbb R^2,$ find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ if $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ as $\mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2.$

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$, where $x_i = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i.$ Computing the components of $\mathbf{x},$ we get the following:

\begin{align*} x_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{2}}=3\sqrt 2 \\[5pt] x_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix}= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}-\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}}=-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=-\sqrt 2 \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} 3\sqrt{2} \\ -\sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}.\]
